skills.name: Plan Mode
skills.description: A restricted primary agent for planning and analysis. By default, file edits and bash commands require approval; Plan is not strictly read-only.
skills.trigger: Press Tab, or use the configured switch_agent keybind, to cycle through primary agents and select Plan
skills.example: Select Plan and ask it to analyze a JWT migration. It proposes an implementation plan; any requested file edit or bash command requires approval. Switch to Build when ready to implement.
skills.howto: Press Tab, or use the configured `switch_agent` keybind, to cycle through primary agents and select Plan. Plan asks for approval before file edits or bash commands by default; configure those permissions as `deny` if strict read-only behavior is required.

skills.name: Undo / Redo
skills.description: Undo removes the latest user message, all subsequent responses, and associated file changes; redo restores a previously undone message. The project must be a Git repository.
skills.example: An unwanted refactor follows the latest prompt → /undo removes that prompt, subsequent responses, and associated file changes → refine the prompt, or use /redo to restore it.
skills.howto: In a Git repository, type /undo to remove the latest user message, all subsequent responses, and associated file changes. Type /redo after /undo to restore the undone message and changes. The default keybinds are `ctrl+x u` and `ctrl+x r`.

skills.name: Agent Skills (SKILL.md)
skills.description: Reusable SKILL.md instructions discovered from project or global OpenCode, Claude-compatible, and agent-compatible skill directories, then loaded on demand through the native skill tool.
skills.trigger: Create .opencode/skills/<name>/SKILL.md with required name and description frontmatter; the name must match its directory
skills.example: A git-release skill appears in the available-skills list → when release work is requested, the agent loads it through the skill tool and follows its instructions.
skills.howto: Create `.opencode/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with required `name` and `description` frontmatter. The lowercase hyphenated name must match its directory. OpenCode also discovers documented global, `.claude/skills/`, and `.agents/skills/` locations; the agent loads a selected skill on demand through the `skill` tool.

skills.name: Session Share
skills.description: Creates a public URL, syncs the session's conversation history to OpenCode's servers, and exposes its messages, responses, and session metadata until it is unshared.
skills.example: After implementing an endpoint, type /share and place the copied public URL in the PR so reviewers can inspect the conversation; use /unshare when review is complete.
skills.howto: Type /share to create a public session URL and copy it to the clipboard. Review the conversation for sensitive information before sharing it. Shared history, messages, responses, and session metadata remain accessible until /unshare removes the link and related data.

skills.name: MCP Server Integration
skills.description: Adds local or remote Model Context Protocol servers whose tools become available to the LLM alongside OpenCode's built-in tools.
skills.trigger: Add a named local or remote server definition under mcp in opencode.json or opencode.jsonc
skills.example: Configure a Postgres MCP server → ask 'show me users created this week' → agent queries the DB directly through the MCP tool without writing a script
skills.howto: Add `mcp.<name>` to `opencode.json` or `opencode.jsonc`. A local server uses a `local` type and a command array; a remote server uses a `remote` type and a URL. MCP tools then appear alongside built-in tools. Set `enabled` to `false` to disable a server.

skills.name: Custom Commands
skills.description: Define custom slash commands for repetitive workflows as markdown files in .opencode/commands/ or in opencode.json.
skills.example: Command 'fix-types' defined as 'Find all TypeScript type errors and fix them without changing logic' → user types /fix-types → agent runs the full workflow immediately
skills.howto: Create `.opencode/commands/<name>.md` or `~/.config/opencode/commands/<name>.md`; optional frontmatter can set `description`, `agent`, and `model`, while the body is the prompt template. Alternatively define `command.<name>` in `opencode.json`. Invoke it as `/<name>` and use `$ARGUMENTS` or positional arguments.

skills.name: GitHub Actions Integration
skills.description: Trigger OpenCode in CI/CD by commenting /opencode or /oc on any GitHub issue or PR. Supports automatic PR review, issue triage, scheduled runs, and code-line comments.
skills.trigger: Comment /opencode <task> or /oc <task> on a GitHub issue or PR
skills.example: Reviewer comments '/opencode add input validation to the form fields in this PR' → agent runs in GitHub Actions → commits the changes → replies with a summary in the PR thread
skills.howto: From a project in a GitHub repository, run `opencode github install`. The wizard installs the OpenCode GitHub App, creates the workflow, and sets up secrets. For manual setup, install the app, add `.github/workflows/opencode.yml`, and configure the required API-key secrets.

skills.name: Custom Agents
skills.description: Defines custom primary or subagents with their own prompt, model, appearance, and permission rules through opencode.json or markdown files.
skills.trigger: Run opencode agent create · or create .opencode/agents/<name>.md with the desired mode, model, prompt, and permissions
skills.example: Create a security-reviewer subagent with edit denied and a security-focused prompt → invoke it with @security-reviewer to audit an endpoint without changing files.
skills.howto: Run `opencode agent create`, or create `.opencode/agents/<name>.md` project-locally or `~/.config/opencode/agents/<name>.md` globally. Supply the required `description`, choose a primary or subagent mode, and configure the model and permissions as needed.

skills.name: LSP Integration
skills.description: Integrates language servers so OpenCode can use diagnostics as feedback for the agent.
skills.trigger: Set lsp to true for all built-in servers, or use an lsp object for built-in overrides and custom servers
skills.example: Enable the appropriate language server → after an edit, OpenCode receives compiler or type diagnostics and uses them as feedback when correcting the code.
skills.howto: Set `lsp` to true in `opencode.json` to enable all built-in LSP servers, or use an `lsp` object for overrides and custom servers. A custom entry uses command and extensions arrays. OpenCode uses resulting diagnostics as agent feedback.

skills.name: Plugins
skills.description: Extends OpenCode through JavaScript or TypeScript plugin functions that hook into events and customize behavior, integrations, or execution.
skills.trigger: Place a plugin in .opencode/plugins/ or ~/.config/opencode/plugins/ · or add an npm package to the plugin array in opencode.json
skills.example: A plugin exports a tool.execute.before hook that validates or modifies bash arguments before the built-in tool executes.
skills.howto: Create a JavaScript or TypeScript module in `.opencode/plugins/` or `~/.config/opencode/plugins/`. Export one or more plugin functions that return event hooks such as `tool.execute.before`, or add npm package names to the `plugin` array in `opencode.json`.

skills.name: Plan Mode
skills.description: Switch the active chat into planning mode so Codex can propose an execution plan before implementation begins.
skills.trigger: Type /plan, optionally followed by the planning request
skills.example: User types '/plan Propose a migration plan for this Express service' → Codex enters plan mode and produces an execution plan.
skills.howto: Type /plan and press Enter, optionally adding the request inline. Codex enters plan mode and uses the inline text as the first planning request. /plan is temporarily unavailable while Codex is already working.

skills.name: Goal Mode
skills.description: Give Codex a durable objective with a verifiable stopping condition. Codex can continue across turns and work independently for multiple hours.
skills.example: User types '/goal Migrate this service to Fastify. Stop when the contract tests pass and the rollback path is documented.' → Codex works through checkpoints toward the stopping condition.
skills.howto: Set a durable objective with /goal <objective>. Use /goal to inspect it and /goal pause, /goal resume, or /goal clear to control it. If the command is missing, enable features.goals in config.toml or run codex features enable goals.

skills.name: Agent Skills (SKILL.md)
skills.description: Reusable workflow directories containing a required SKILL.md and optional scripts, references, assets, and metadata. Codex loads full instructions when a skill is selected.
skills.trigger: Run /skills or type $ to mention a skill in CLI/IDE · or describe a task matching its description
skills.example: A repository skill documents the release workflow → the user asks Codex to prepare a release → Codex selects and follows the skill.
skills.howto: Create `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` with name and description metadata. Codex scans repository skill directories from the current directory to the repository root; user skills can live in `~/.agents/skills`. In CLI/IDE, invoke a skill explicitly with $ or /skills, or let Codex match its description implicitly.

skills.name: Skill Creator
skills.description: A bundled system skill that asks what a skill should do, when it should trigger, and whether it should remain instruction-only or include scripts.
skills.example: User invokes $skill-creator → describes a deployment workflow and its triggers → reviews the generated skill.
skills.howto: Invoke $skill-creator and answer its questions about purpose, triggers, and scripts. Review the generated skill and place it in a supported repository or user skill location. Codex detects changes automatically; restart only if the skill does not appear.

skills.name: Skill Installer
skills.description: A bundled system skill for installing curated skills or downloading skills from other repositories into the user's local Codex setup.
skills.example: User types '$skill-installer linear' → Codex installs the curated Linear skill for local use.
skills.howto: Run $skill-installer followed by a curated skill name, such as $skill-installer linear, or ask it to download a skill from another repository. Codex detects installed skills automatically; restart only if one does not appear.

skills.name: Thread Automations
skills.description: Heartbeat-style recurring wake-ups attached to the current thread. They preserve thread context and support minute-based intervals or daily and weekly schedules.
skills.trigger: Ask Codex in the current thread to create an automation with a task and schedule
skills.example: A thread automation checks a long-running command every few minutes until it finishes, then reports in the same conversation.
skills.howto: In a regular thread, ask Codex to create a thread automation and specify the task, schedule, reporting rules, and stopping condition. Test the prompt manually first. Manage automations from the Automations pane in the app sidebar.

skills.name: Chats
skills.description: Threads for tasks that do not need a specific project folder or Git repository, including research, triage, planning, and connected-tool workflows.
skills.trigger: Start a Chat when the task is not tied to a codebase
skills.example: User starts a Chat to research an API through connected tools without opening a repository.
skills.howto: Start a Chat for research, triage, planning, connected-tool work, or another task that does not require a project folder or Git repository.

skills.name: Worktree Mode
skills.description: Create a new Git worktree so Codex changes remain isolated from the regular project checkout and independent tasks can run side by side.
skills.trigger: Choose Worktree when creating a new thread
skills.example: User runs a risky refactor in a worktree → reviews the isolated diff → uses the app's Git tools as appropriate.
skills.howto: Choose Worktree instead of Local when creating the thread. Codex creates an isolated Git worktree. Review the resulting diff and use the built-in Git tools to stage, revert, commit, push, or create a pull request as needed.

skills.name: MCP Server Integration
skills.description: Connect external tools and services through Model Context Protocol servers. The Codex app, CLI, and IDE extension use the same MCP configuration.
skills.trigger: Open the MCP section in app settings · or configure MCP in config.toml
skills.example: User enables a recommended MCP server → Codex can call that server's tools from supported Codex surfaces.
skills.howto: Open the MCP section in the app settings and enable a recommended server or add a custom server. The app, CLI, and IDE extension use the same MCP configuration stored in `config.toml`.

skills.name: Voice Dictation
skills.description: Transcribe microphone input into an editable Codex prompt.
skills.trigger: Hold Ctrl+M while the composer is visible
skills.example: User holds Ctrl+M and dictates a task → reviews or edits the transcription → sends it to start work.
skills.howto: With the composer visible, hold Ctrl+M and speak. Review or edit the transcription, then send it to start the task.

skills.name: Steering & Queuing
skills.description: In the IDE extension, follow-up messages sent during a run can either wait for the next run in queue mode or modify the current run in steer mode.
skills.trigger: Set chatgpt.followUpQueueMode to queue or steer · use Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+Enter to invert it for one message
skills.example: With queue as the default, a follow-up waits for the next run → Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+Enter sends one follow-up as steering instead.
skills.howto: Set `chatgpt.followUpQueueMode` to `queue` or `steer` in the IDE extension. During a run, send the follow-up normally for the configured behavior, or press Cmd/Ctrl+Shift+Enter to invert it for that message.

skills.name: Memories
skills.description: An opt-in local recall layer that can carry stable preferences, recurring workflows, technology choices, project conventions, and known pitfalls from eligible earlier threads into future work.
skills.trigger: Enable Memories in settings · or set memories = true under [features] in ~/.codex/config.toml
skills.example: After Memories is enabled, Codex can recall a stable project convention from eligible earlier threads without treating it as mandatory team policy.
skills.howto: Enable Memories in Codex settings or `config.toml`. Use /memories to control whether the current thread uses existing memories or contributes future memories. Keep mandatory team rules in AGENTS.md or checked-in documentation; generated memory state lives under `~/.codex/memories/`.

skills.name: Compaction
skills.description: Auto-summarises older context when it approaches the model's window so long sessions stay alive without losing the work, with a structured goal, progress, and file-tracker format the model can pick up from.
skills.trigger: /compact · auto when contextWindow - reserveTokens is exceeded
skills.howto: Run /compact [instructions] to summarize older messages manually; configure reserveTokens and keepRecentTokens in ~/.pi/agent/settings.json or <project-dir>/.pi/settings.json.
skills.example: A long debugging session reaches the configured threshold and compacts older messages into a structured summary while retaining recent context.

skills.name: Extensions
skills.description: TypeScript modules that register custom tools, slash commands, event handlers, and TUI components on the ExtensionAPI, with full access to the session, settings, and provider layer.
skills.trigger: export default function (pi: ExtensionAPI) { ... } in an extensions/ folder
skills.howto: Place a TypeScript extension in ~/.pi/agent/extensions/ or .pi/extensions/, then run /reload; use pi -e ./path.ts only for quick tests.
skills.example: An extension hooks session_before_compact to generate summaries with your own model, replacing the default LLM call and keeping the LLM-agnostic summarization pipeline.

skills.name: Skills (Agent Skills standard)
skills.description: Self-contained capability packages that follow the Agent Skills spec and load on demand with progressive disclosure, so only the descriptions are always in context and full instructions arrive when matched.
skills.trigger: Put SKILL.md in ~/.pi/agent/skills/<name>/ or .pi/skills/<name>/ · use --skill <path> for explicit loading
skills.howto: Put SKILL.md inside a skill directory under ~/.pi/agent/skills/ or the trusted project's .pi/skills/; use repeatable --skill <path> arguments for explicit loading.
skills.example: A brave-search skill appears in the available-skills list, and the model loads its full SKILL.md only when the task needs a web lookup.

skills.name: Prompt templates
skills.description: Reusable markdown prompts that expand from slash commands, parameterised with $1, $2 positional args and $ARGUMENTS for the full input, shipped with the agent or defined in prompts/ directories.
skills.trigger: /template-name with args · register a .md file under prompts/
skills.howto: Create a Markdown file such as ~/.pi/agent/prompts/review.md or .pi/prompts/review.md, then invoke it as /review; optionally add description and argument-hint frontmatter.
skills.example: /review-pr diff expands a saved template that diffs the current branch, scans for anti-patterns, and produces a structured code review every time without re-writing the prompt from scratch.

skills.name: Pi packages
skills.description: Bundle and share extensions, skills, prompt templates, and themes through npm or git so a single install brings the whole capability surface, with optional per-resource filtering.
skills.trigger: pi install npm:@you/your-pkg · pi install git:github.com/you/repo@v1 · pi install ./path
skills.howto: Run pi install npm:@foo/bar@1.0.0, or install from a git reference, URL, or local path; add -l when installation should be recorded in .pi/settings.json instead of ~/.pi/agent/settings.json.
skills.example: pi install npm:@badlogic/pi-brave-search adds the search skill and the matching extension in one shot, pinned to a specific version, and the project auto-installs its missing packages on next startup.

skills.name: Sessions
skills.description: Persistent JSONL sessions with /tree branching, /fork, /clone, named sessions, searchable /resume, and one-click export to HTML or a private GitHub gist with a read-only share link.
skills.howto: Run pi -c to continue the most recent session or pi -r to browse previous sessions; use pi --no-session for an unsaved session.
skills.example: pi -r opens a searchable picker of every past session in the current project, then /share publishes a chosen session as a private GitHub gist and returns a read-only HTML link the team can browse.

skills.name: Multi-provider
skills.description: One CLI for every major model — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Groq, DeepSeek, Mistral, Cerebras, plus ChatGPT Plus, Claude Pro, and GitHub Copilot subscriptions through /login.
skills.howto: Run /login and select a provider to configure subscription OAuth or an API key; alternatively export a provider variable such as ANTHROPIC_API_KEY before starting pi, and use /logout to clear stored credentials.
skills.example: Run /login to authenticate with ChatGPT Plus for OpenAI Codex, then switch to Claude Pro for the next session — no code changes, no swapping CLIs, no rewriting prompts to fit a different harness.

skills.name: Custom providers
skills.description: Register your own model API via pi.registerProvider() for corporate proxies, self-hosted deployments, OAuth flows, and non-standard LLM APIs, with full streaming and tool-calling support.
skills.howto: In an extension factory, call pi.registerProvider("my-provider", { name, baseUrl, apiKey: "$MY_API_KEY", api, models }) and register dynamically discovered models there rather than during session_start.
skills.example: An extension routes Anthropic traffic through a corporate gateway by registering the existing provider with a custom baseUrl and auth headers, so every request leaves the network through the approved path.
